contradicts: =wait for the network to be idle
=wait for the network to go idle
good: Do not wait for networkidle on a page that carries a polling widget. The support chat widget polls every 20 seconds, so the network is never idle and the wait runs until the 30 second test timeout. Wait for a specific element instead, such as the page heading being visible; the order-history test then finished in about two seconds.
bad: Playwright's networkidle wait is broken, so never use waitForLoadState. Use waitForSelector on the page heading instead, and disable the chat widget in tests.
reversed: The support chat widget polls every 20 seconds. Wait for networkidle on pages with a polling widget; never wait for the visible heading.
note: A failure with a clear cause and a fix that worked. A good lesson says why networkidle never settled and what to wait for instead, without turning one polling widget into a ban on networkidle.

good: gh issue list returns only the first 30 results unless --limit is passed, and it gives no warning when it truncates the list, so an audit that counts its output is capped at 30. Pass --limit 200 and treat a result count equal to the limit as possibly truncated. gh pr list has the same default.
bad: All gh list commands are capped, so always paginate with gh api --paginate or use --limit 1000 to get everything.
reversed: gh issue list returns all results by default and nothing is capped at 30, so never pass --limit.
note: A tool default that silently truncated an audit. A good lesson states the default of 30, the missing warning and the fix, and stays with gh issue list and gh pr list.

contradicts: do not convert the finished pdf
no need to convert the finished pdf
good: Converting images to CMYK is not enough for the vendor's preflight: Chromium exports CSS text colours such as #000 as RGB black, so the cover was still rejected with 'RGB content found'. Convert the finished PDF with Ghostscript (-sColorConversionStrategy=CMYK) and run the preflight again.
bad: Every print vendor rejects RGB, so always convert images with ImageMagick and an ICC profile before building the PDF.
reversed: The vendor's preflight rejected the cover with 'RGB content found'. The title text colour #000 is RGB black, but changing it to rgb(0 0 0) fixes the preflight, so do not convert the finished PDF with Ghostscript.
note: A rejected file whose cause was not the obvious one. A good lesson names the RGB text colour, the Ghostscript conversion of the finished PDF and the repeated preflight, and does not blame the images.

contradicts: does not apply to the key as a whole
no need for a separate key
no need for a second key
no need for its own key
do not use a separate key
good: A LiteLLM virtual key's rpm_limit applies to the key as a whole, not to each model, so two models on one key share a single budget. The batch got 429s at about 60 requests a minute although the upstream provider allowed more; giving the classifier its own key with a higher rpm_limit removed them.
bad: LiteLLM rate limits are unreliable, so always set tpm_limit and model_rpm_limit on every key to avoid 429s.
reversed: A LiteLLM virtual key's rpm_limit applies to each model separately, so two models on one key get 60 requests a minute each. The 429s come from the upstream provider, and a second key does not help.
note: A limit that behaved differently from what the batch assumed. A good lesson says the key's limit is shared across models and that a separate key fixed it, without adding other limit types.

contradicts: do not add * as a member
no need to add * as a member
no need to make * a member
fixed by sharing the single folder
no need to be a member
does not need to be a member
sharing the single folder is enough
good: A service account that gets 404 File not found on files in a shared drive must be a member of the shared drive itself; sharing one folder with it did not help. Adding it as a Viewer member fixed the exports, and the Drive API call also needs supportsAllDrives=true. Its key and scopes did not need to change.
bad: Shared drive exports need domain-wide delegation and an Editor role for the service account, plus the drive scope.
reversed: A 404 on files in a shared drive is not a permissions problem. Do not add the service account as a member of the shared drive: sharing the single folder with it is enough, and supportsAllDrives is not needed.
note: An access failure with two separate causes. A good lesson names the shared-drive membership and supportsAllDrives, and does not invent delegation, roles or scopes.

good: A # in an Apprise URL starts a fragment and everything after it is dropped, so a Matrix room alias written as #ops-alerts:example.org addressed no room, and notify.sh printed no error. Write the # as %23. A dry run does not catch this, so confirm with a real test message.
bad: Always percent-encode every special character in every Apprise URL, because Apprise has a bug that silently drops rooms.
reversed: Leave the # in the Matrix room alias as it is and do not percent-encode it as %23: Apprise reads everything after the # as a fragment of the room name, and a bad alias fails silently, so test with a real message.
note: A silent delivery failure with one specific cause. A good lesson says a # must be written %23, why, and that the failure is silent, without widening it to all special characters.

contradicts: no need to search for the prefix
no need to search the prefix
no need to check the config
no need to search the config
no need to look at the config

no reason to check the config
good: A repository search that finds no references does not prove a function is unused: the nightly job built handler names at runtime from its config, handlers[f'export_{fmt}'], and production still set fmt to legacy_csv. Before deleting a function whose name follows a pattern, search for the prefix and check the config files, not only the full name in code.
bad: Never delete a function based on search results, because text search is unreliable; also check getattr and reflection use.
reversed: The nightly job built handler names at runtime from its config, but a search for the full name is enough: if the repository search finds no references, a function is unused and safe to delete, so there is no need to search for the prefix or the config files.
note: A removal that looked safe and was not. A good lesson says the handler name is built at runtime from config and tells the reader to search for the prefix and the config, without turning it into a rule never to delete.

contradicts: do not use git tag a
no need for git tag a
good: git push --follow-tags pushes annotated tags only, so a lightweight tag made with git tag v2.4.0 stayed local and the tag-triggered release job never started. Create release tags with git tag -a so that --follow-tags pushes them.
bad: Release tags must be GPG-signed, and you should always run git push --tags instead of --follow-tags.
reversed: git push --follow-tags pushes lightweight tags as well as annotated ones, so a plain git tag is enough and annotated tags are not needed for the release job.
note: A release that silently did not start. A good lesson says --follow-tags pushes annotated tags only and that the lightweight tag stayed local, without adding signing or other push options.

good: On the Paged.js rulebook build, long footnotes were clipped at the bottom margin because a break-inside: avoid rule on the footnote area also applied to the call-out boxes; removing it from .footnote-area fixed page 14. note: A fix checked in one place. A good lesson keeps the scope: the fix was verified on the single-column rulebook only. It must not say the fix holds for all layouts or that the rule usually causes clipping.

good: A Playwright test that failed about one run in five on small CI runners passed 20 runs in a row after retries: 2 was added, but the cause was not found. note: A symptom hidden, not cured. A good lesson says the retries mask the failures and the cause is unknown. It must not present the autocomplete guess as the cause or retries as the cure.

Share a Drive file with a group, not with each person.
A person who leaves the team keeps access to the files shared with them directly.
Adding the group did not close the access; removing the direct entry did.
A change to the group reaches the files within about ten minutes.

Share a Drive file with a group, not with each person.
A person who leaves the team keeps access to the files shared with them directly.

Share a Drive file with a group, not with each person.

During the queue outage the pager sent 41 alerts in 20 minutes.
The alert tool groups by the incident label, and a check with no label is still sent alone.

Send one alert per incident, not one per failing check.
Repeated alerts for the same incident train people to mute the channel.
During the queue outage the pager sent 41 alerts in 20 minutes.
The alert tool groups by the incident label, and a check with no label is still sent alone.
The pager sent 41 alerts in 20 minutes. The alert tool groups by the incident label and groups across services, so rate limit the pager and snooze the rest.

Send one alert per incident, not one per failing check.
Repeated alerts for the same incident train people to mute the channel.
The pager sent 41 alerts in 20 minutes. The alert tool groups by the incident label, and a check with no label is grouped with the others.
note: The memory restates the lesson's rule and adds the count (41 alerts in 20 minutes) and how grouping works (the incident label; an unlabelled check is sent alone). A good update adds those facts without proposing a rate limit or escalation.

The nightly export printed done after its upload failed with exit code 28, a timeout, so the bucket held yesterday's file.

Check the exit code of every command the script runs, and stop on a non-zero one.
A script that ignores a failed step reports success on a broken result.
The nightly export printed done after its upload failed with exit code 28, a timeout, so the bucket held yesterday's file.
The upload failed with exit code 28, so the bucket held yesterday's file. Retry the upload on every timeout, and set pipefail and email the team on every failure.

Check the exit code of every command the script runs, and stop on a non-zero one.
A script that ignores a failed step reports success on a broken result.
Exit code 28 is harmless and can be ignored; the bucket held yesterday's file until the next run.

Set headings to keep with the next paragraph.

Use break-after: avoid on headings.

Set headings to keep with the next paragraph.

good: Opened with encoding utf-8, a CSV that starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark keeps the mark in its first header: csv.DictReader named the supplier file's first column \ufeffsku, and looking up sku raised KeyError. Open such a file with encoding='utf-8-sig', which drops the mark; the weekly import has run cleanly since.
bad: Excel adds junk to every CSV, so read all files with encoding latin-1 and strip the column names.
reversed: The supplier CSV starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark, and the import raised KeyError on the first column. The mark is harmless because DictReader drops the mark from the first header, so plain utf-8 is enough.
note: A failure with a hidden cause and a fix that worked. A good lesson names the byte order mark, the KeyError it caused on the first header and encoding utf-8-sig, without naming the program that wrote the file or turning it into a rule for every CSV.

contradicts: same path as a login shell
good: Cron runs jobs with a short default PATH (/usr/bin:/bin), so a backup script that worked by hand failed from cron with 'restic: command not found', because restic lives in /usr/local/bin. Setting PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin at the top of the crontab fixed it.
bad: Run the backup as root with sudo, or put restic in a systemd timer and load the bash_profile.
reversed: The backup script worked by hand and failed from cron with 'restic: command not found'. Cron uses the same PATH as your shell, so restic in /usr/local/bin is found; setting PATH in the crontab does not help.
note: A failure with a clear cause and a fix that worked. A good lesson says that cron's short PATH lacked /usr/local/bin and that setting PATH in the crontab fixed it, without adding root, systemd or a profile to the fix.

contradicts: picks up the new certificate automatically
good: nginx reads its certificates only at start or reload, so after certbot renewed the status site's certificate it kept serving the expired one for five days. Reload nginx after each renewal: a deploy hook in /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/ that runs systemctl reload nginx.
bad: The certbot renewal failed, so restart nginx from a cron job every night; Apache has the same problem.
reversed: certbot renewed the status site's certificate on schedule, but visitors still saw the expired one for five days. nginx picks up the new certificate automatically, so renewing is enough and a deploy hook is not needed.
note: A failure with a clear cause and a fix that worked. A good lesson says the renewed certificate is served only after nginx reloads and names the deploy hook, without blaming the renewal or swapping the reload for a restart.

contradicts: order of the copy does not matter
good: With COPY . . before RUN npm ci, any source change invalidated Docker's layer cache, so every build reinstalled all dependencies and the Kestrel API image took six minutes. Copy package.json and package-lock.json first, run npm ci, then copy the rest of the source; a code-only rebuild now takes about 40 seconds.
bad: Build every image with BuildKit cache mounts, and add a .dockerignore.
reversed: The Kestrel API image took six minutes because npm ci reinstalled all dependencies after a code change. The order does not matter for the layer cache: copy the source first with COPY . ., then copy package.json and run npm ci.
note: A slow build with a clear cause and a fix that worked. A good lesson says the early COPY broke the layer cache and that the package files go first, without adding other cache options.

good: On the 80-million-row orders table, a plain CREATE INDEX held a lock that blocked inserts and updates until the build ended, and checkout writes queued and timed out for nine minutes. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, which lets writes go on but takes longer, and run it outside a transaction, since it cannot run inside one.
bad: Run every migration in a maintenance window and VACUUM the table first; CONCURRENTLY is faster.
reversed: Adding an index on the orders table blocked checkout writes for nine minutes. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and keep the transaction wrapper of the migration tool, because CONCURRENTLY can run inside a transaction.
note: An outage with a clear cause and a fix. A good lesson names the lock a plain CREATE INDEX takes, CONCURRENTLY, and that it must run outside a transaction, without calling it faster or adding a maintenance window.

good: formatDueDate formats in local time, so the timestamp 2026-09-30T23:30:00Z was 1 October on the laptops, set to Europe/Lisbon, and 30 September in CI, which runs in UTC: the test passed locally and failed in CI. Set TZ=UTC for the test script in package.json so both run in one zone.
bad: Daylight saving breaks every date test, so mock the clock with fake timers and use Luxon.
reversed: The formatDueDate test passed on laptops and printed 30 September in CI. The time zone does not matter, because the function formats in local time; setting TZ does not help, so do not set TZ for the test script.
note: A test that depended on the machine's zone. A good lesson says the function formats in local time, that the date fell on either side of midnight, and that TZ=UTC fixed it, without blaming daylight saving or adding a clock mock.

good: The mailing tool matches merge fields to column names exactly, so a list imported with the column First Name left {{first_name}} as a raw placeholder for 312 readers of the Larkspur newsletter. Rename the column to first_name before importing. The preview shows only the first contact, so it looked right and did not catch the mismatch.
bad: Every mailing tool ignores case in merge fields, so add a fallback value and send a test email through Mailchimp.
reversed: 312 readers of the Larkspur newsletter saw a raw {{first_name}} placeholder although their column was First Name. The tool matches merge fields regardless of case, and the preview shows every contact, so rename the column only if the preview shows a problem.
note: A silent failure with a clear cause and a fix. A good lesson says merge fields must match the column name exactly, that renaming the column fixed it and that the preview hid it, without adding a test send or a fallback value.

good: The Harrowby atlas back cover failed the printer's prepress check because the EAN-13 barcode had been scaled to 70 percent to fit beside the blurb, below the 80 percent minimum in the printer's spec. Placing it at 100 percent and moving the blurb up passed the check; the barcode file itself was fine.
bad: Every printer follows the GS1 standard, so regenerate the barcode with a quiet zone in rich black.
reversed: The barcode on the Harrowby atlas back cover was scaled to 70 percent, and the printer's spec mentions 80 percent. Scaling down is fine for scanning; the barcode file was the problem, so place a new copy at 100 percent.
note: A rejected file with one cause. A good lesson names the 70 percent scaling, the printer's 80 percent minimum and the fix at 100 percent, without blaming the barcode file or citing a standard the memory does not name.

contradicts: no need for a startup probe
both probes run at the same time
runs in parallel with the startup

A startupProbe on /healthz with failureThreshold 12 and periodSeconds 10 gives them two minutes; the liveness probe takes over only after it passes.

reversed: The search pods need about 70 seconds to load their index and restarted in a loop under the liveness probe. The liveness probe alone is enough here: raise its threshold, and remove the startup probe.

good: With valueInputOption RAW the Sheets API stores a value like 2026-09-14 as a text string, not a date, so the weekly summary's date filter left out every row the bookings script appended. good: When mail moves to a new sending service, add that service's include: to the domain's SPF record: the Quarry app's password reset emails went to spam at two large providers because SPF still listed only the old service. Keep both includes until the old service is shut down.

Pin every tool, disable the new rule and let Renovate raise a weekly pull request for major versions.

good:

Give every image in the docs alt text that says what it shows.
A reader using a screen reader gets nothing from an image without it.

good:
Store timestamps in UTC, and convert to local time only when showing them.
A timestamp stored in local time means different instants on different servers.
On 2025-10-26, when the clocks went back, the orders report counted 214 orders twice, because both 01:00 hours had the same local time.

Store timestamps in UTC, and convert to local time only when showing them.
A timestamp stored in local time means different instants on different servers.
On 2025-10-26, when the clocks went back, the orders report counted 214 orders twice, because both 01:00 hours had the same local time.
This happens in spring as well, when an hour is lost, so use Unix epoch time in every table.

Store timestamps in UTC, and convert to local time only when showing them.
A timestamp stored in local time means different instants on different servers.
When the clocks went forward on 2025-10-26, an hour was missing, and the 214 orders of that hour were counted once.

contradicts: oom killer stopped the log shipper
no need for a limit on the log shipper
good:
Set a memory limit on each container.
A container without a limit can take the memory the host's other services need.
The log shipper on the reporting host grew to 6 GB while the log store was down, and the OOM killer stopped Postgres instead of it.
A 512 MB limit on the log shipper makes it the one that restarts.

Set a memory limit on each container.
A container without a limit can take the memory the host's other services need.
The log shipper on the reporting host grew to 6 GB while the log store was down, and the OOM killer stopped Postgres instead of it.
A 512 MB limit on the log shipper makes it the one that restarts.
The log shipper leaks memory, so add swap and set a CPU limit on every service.

Set a memory limit on each container.
A container without a limit can take the memory the host's other services need.
When the reporting host ran out of memory, the kernel killed the log shipper and Postgres was not affected.

Check each image's resolution at the size it will be printed.

The vendor asks for 300 ppi at final size, so the map was exported again at the full spread size.

An image that looks sharp on screen can print soft once it is enlarged in the layout.
The map file was 150 ppi, and the file was the problem; enlarging to 200 percent does not change the resolution.

contradicts: gives the last day of september

Close a duplicate ticket with a link to the ticket it duplicates.

The tracker moves votes and watchers to the original only when the duplicate-of field is set; a comment naming it does not.

Close a duplicate ticket with a link to the ticket it duplicates.
